headline: Massachusetts approves sprinkler checks after deadly Fall River fire
dek: New statewide requirements will require annual checks for recalled sprinkler heads and give local fire departments added authority while the code changes move toward adoption next year.
body: Massachusetts regulators have approved new fire-safety requirements aimed at preventing a repeat of the deadly Gabriel House fire in Fall River, putting recalled sprinkler equipment at the center of a statewide code update. The Board of Fire Prevention Regulations voted Oct. 15 to include the provisions in the next edition of the Massachusetts Comprehensive Fire Safety Code, which the Healey administration expects to publish early next year. The [state announcement](https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-announces-new-fire-safety-requirements-approved-to-protect-massachusetts-residents) describes the action as a response to a tragedy that exposed the consequences of treating a sprinkler inspection as complete without confirming that the devices can function.

The new requirements will require sprinkler systems to undergo an annual check for recalled sprinkler heads. When recalled equipment is found, the property owner must notify the local fire department and ensure that the equipment is replaced promptly. Until replacement occurs, the local department will be able to require additional fire-protection measures. Those provisions are important because they add a communication step between a building owner and the community's fire-safety authorities rather than leaving a recall as a private maintenance issue.

The changes grew out of a recommendation from Fall River Fire Captain Joshua Hetzler after the Gabriel House fire. The assisted-living facility suffered a five-alarm fire on July 13, 2025, that killed 10 people and forced the evacuation of more than 50 other residents, according to the state. [Boston 25 News](https://cmg-cmg-tv-10020-prod.cdn.arcpublishing.com/news/local/gov-healey-announces-new-fire-safety-regulations-following-deadly-gabriel-house-fire/O2RI3DOVXVDBREAKO6YB4YFOJA/) reported that the blaze was the deadliest fire in Massachusetts in more than 40 years and that 30 people were injured. The regulation vote therefore has a direct Fall River origin but affects buildings across the Commonwealth.

The underlying concern is not simply whether a facility has sprinklers on paper. The Boston Globe reported in July that Gabriel House used sprinkler heads subject to a 2001 recall involving defective O-ring seals that could keep a device from activating during an emergency. The Globe also reported that the same type of recalled heads had been found at six other shared-housing properties in Fall River and five in neighboring New Bedford, with those devices later replaced. That history helps explain why the new rule focuses specifically on recall identification and notice to fire departments.

The state announcement says the revised code also builds on earlier administration steps to strengthen emergency preparedness and accountability at assisted-living residences. Boston 25 reported additional provisions involving certain welding and grinding work when winds exceed 15 miles per hour, as well as efforts to simplify building-permitting and certification requirements. Those elements broaden the package beyond sprinkler heads, but the recall-check provision is the part most directly connected to the Gabriel House investigation and to the recommendation brought forward by Fall River firefighters.

The rules are not yet an immediate replacement mandate for every sprinkler head in Massachusetts. The board's vote places the requirements in the next code edition, and the administration's announcement gives early next year as the expected publication point. It does not provide a facility-by-facility inventory of recalled equipment, a statewide cost estimate or a date by which every affected property must complete its first new check. Those details will matter to assisted-living operators, housing providers and local fire departments planning inspections and replacement work.

The policy also changes who must know about a problem. Under the framework described by the state, an owner remains responsible for correcting recalled equipment, while the local fire department gains notice and the ability to demand interim safeguards. That could include measures that vary by building and risk, so the final code language will determine how departments apply the authority. The approach reflects the practical lesson from Fall River: a warning about a defective component is only protective if it leads to a documented correction or to temporary steps that reduce the danger while repairs are pending.

For families evaluating assisted-living residences, the update is a safety standard in progress rather than a guarantee that every facility already meets the coming requirements. The state says the new code will strengthen protections for residents, and independent reporting has documented why recalled sprinklers became a focus. The next checkpoints are publication of the revised code, guidance to owners and fire departments, and evidence that annual checks are completed and recalled equipment is replaced. Until then, Massachusetts has approved the direction of the reform, but the operational details remain to be finalized.
